'''To wear on''' or '''upon†''', to have on; wear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Therfore I made my visitaciouns, . . .

{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 559.}}}}

'''wear<sup>1</sup>''' (wãr), ''n.'' [< ''wear''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The act of wearing or using, or the state of being worn or used, as garments, ornaments, etc.; use: as, a garment not for every-day ''wear''.
{{smaller block|They have a great manufacture of coarse woollen cloth in and about Salonica, which is exported to all parts of Turky for the ''wear'' of common people.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 151.}}
He had transferred all the contents of his every-day pockets to those actually in ''wear.''
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' Stuff or material for articles of wear; material for garments, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Nor.'' What ’s in that pack there?
''First Sold.'' ’Tis English cloth.
''Nor.'' That ’s a good ''wear'' indeed.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, ii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' An article or articles worn, or intended or fit to be worn; style of dress, adornment, or the like; hence, fashion; vogue.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''weare''' (wēr), ''n.'' [A spelling of ''wear''<sup>3</sup>, ''weir.''] In ''her.'', a bearing representing a screen or fence made of wattled twigs, or the like, and upright stakes. It is generally represented in fesse.

'''wearer''' (wãr′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''wear''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who wears, bears, or carries on the body, or as an appendage to the body: as, the ''wearer'' of a cloak, a sword, or a crown.
{{smaller block|<poem>By Jupiter,
Were I the ''wearer'' of Antonius’ beard,
I would not shave ’t to-day.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 2. 7.}}
<poem>Cowls, hoods, and habits, with their ''wearers'' toss’d
And flutter’d into rags.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 490.}}}}
'''2.''' That which wears, wastes, or consumes: as, the waves are the patient ''wearers'' of the rocks.

'''weariable''' (wēr′i-ạ-bl), ''a.'' [< ''weary''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able.''] Capable of becoming wearied or fatigued. ''Quarterly Rev.'' [Rare.]

'''wearied''' (wēr′id), ''p. a.'' Tired; fatigued; exhausted with exertion.
{{smaller block|The Samoeds know these vnknowne deserts, and can tell where the mosse groweth wherewith they refresh their ''wearied'' Deere.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 434.}}}}

'''weariful''' (wēr′i-fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''weary''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful.''] An unnecessary extension of ''weary''<sup>1</sup>; perhaps suggested by ''wearisome.''] Full of weariness; causing weariness; wearisome; tiresome; tedious. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I was reading “Polexandre,” the ''wearifullest'' of books, I think; and I heard nothing but the rats and the mice.
{{right|''A. E. Barr'', Friend Olivia, ii.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''wearifully''' (wēr′i-fůl-i), ''adv.'' In a weariful manner; wearisomely. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The long night passed slowly and ''wearifully.''
{{right|''W. Black,'' In Far Lochaber, xxiii.}}}}

'''weariless''' (wēr′i-les), ''a.'' [< ''weary'' + ''-less.''] Incessant; unwearying; unwearied: as, ''weariless'' wings. ''Hogg.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Beaten and packed
With the flashing flails of ''weariless'' seas.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell,'' Appledore, iii.}}}}

'''wearily''' (wēr′i-li), ''adv.'' In a weary manner; like one fatigued.
{{smaller block|You look ''wearily.'' {{right|''Shak.,'' Tempest, iii. 1. 32.}}}}

'''weariness''' (wēr′i-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''werynes, werinesse, werynesse, werinisse,'' < AS. ''wērignes, wērines,'' weariness, < ''wērig,'' weary: see ''weary'' and ''-ness.''] '''1.''' The state of being weary or tired; that lassitude or exhaustion of strength which is induced by labor, or lack of sleep or rest; fatigue.
{{smaller block|<poem>After his hunteng and his besynesse,
ffor his travell and his grete ''werynes,''
He felle a slepe. ''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 160.</poem>
We come to a certayne stone vpon ye which our blessyd Lady was wont to rest her ''werynes'' whan she most deuoutly visyted these holy place[s] after ye ascension of or Lord.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde,'' Pylgrymage, p. 33.}}
<poem>''Weariness''
Can snore upon the flint, when resty sloth
Finds the down pillow hard.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' Cymbeline, iii. 6. 33.}}
With ''weariness'' and wine oppress’d.
{{right|''Dryden,'' tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xii. 763.}}}}
'''2.''' Mental depression proceeding from monotonous continuance; tedium; ennui; languor.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wear|6860|wearisome}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|''Wear out'' thy youth with shapeless idleness.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 1. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|Tears, sighs, and groans you shall ''wear out'' your days with.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller|Hence—(''c'') To obliterate; efface.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Men that are bred in blood have no way left ’em,
No bath, no purge, no time to ''wear it out''
Or wash it off, but penitence and prayer.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Who have almost ''worn out'' all the impressions of the work of the Law written in their hearts.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. ii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') To harass; tire completely; fatigue; exhaust; waste or consume the strength of.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Stunn’d and ''worn out'' with endless Chat.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Alma, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|“Here,” said I to an old soldier with one hand, who had been campaign’d, and ''worn out'' to death in the service, “here ’s a couple of sous for thee.”
{{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey, Montriul.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To wear the breeches.''' See ''breeches.''—'''To wear the willow.''' See ''willow''<sup>1</sup>, 1.—'''To wear yellow hose''' or '''stockings†.''' See ''yellow.''}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To be in fashion; be in common or recognized use.
{{smaller block|Like the brooch and the tooth-pick, which ''wear'' not now.
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, i. 1. 172.}}}}
'''2†.''' To become fit or suitable by use; become accustomed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Let still the woman take
An elder than herself; so ''wears'' she to him;
So sways she level in her husband’s heart.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 4. 31.}}}}
'''3.''' To last or hold out in course of use or the lapse of time: generally with ''well'' or ''ill''.
{{smaller block|The flattery with which he began, in telling me how ''well'' I ''wore'', was not disagreeable.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 208.}}}}

'''4.''' To undergo gradual impairment or diminution through use, attrition, or lapse of time; waste or diminish gradually; become obliterated: often with ''away'', ''off'', or ''out''.
{{smaller block|Thou wilt surely ''wear away''. {{right|Ex. xviii. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|Though marble ''wear'' with raining.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 560.}}}}
{{smaller block|The suffering plough-share or the flint may ''wear''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Love, like some Stains, will ''wear out'' of it self.
{{right|''Etherege'', She Would if She Could, v. 1}}}}
{{smaller block|If passion causes a present terror, yet it soon ''wears off''.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
{{smaller block|They showed him all manner of furniture which their Lord had provided for pilgrims, as sword, shield, helmet, breast-plate, all-prayer, and shoes that would not ''wear out''.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}

'''5.''' To pass or be spent; become gradually consumed or exhausted.
{{smaller block|Away, I say; time ''wears''. ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 1. 8.
<poem>The day ''wears'';
And those that have been offering early prayers
Are now retiring homeward.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The day ''wears'' away; if you think good, let us prepare to be going. {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}}}

'''6.''' To move or advance slowly; make gradual progress: as, the winter ''wore'' on.
{{smaller block|<poem>Never morning ''wore''
To evening but some heart did break.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|As time ''wore'' on and the offices were filled, the throng of eager aspirants diminished and faded away.
{{right|''The Century'', XLI. 33.}}}} '''7.''' To become; grow. [Old Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|The Spaniards began to ''ware'' weary, for winter drew on.
{{right|''Berners.''}}}}
'''8.''' ''Naut.'', to come round with the head away from the wind: said of a ship.
{{smaller block|The helm was hard up, the after yards shaking, and the ship in the act of ''wearing.''
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 372.}}}}

'''To wear on''' or '''upon†''', to have on; wear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Therfore I made my visitaciouns, . . .
And ''wered upon'' my gaye scarlet gytes.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 559.}}}}

'''wear<sup>1</sup>''' (wãr), ''n.''   [< ''wear''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of wearing or using, or the state of being worn or used, as garments, ornaments, etc.; use: as, a garment not for every-day ''wear''.
{{smaller block|They have a great manufacture of coarse woollen cloth in and about Salonica, which is exported to all parts of Turky for the ''wear'' of common people.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 151.}}}}
{{smaller block|He had transferred all the contents of his every-day pockets to those actually in ''wear.''
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' Stuff or material for articles of wear; material for garments, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Nor.'' What ’s in that pack there?
''First Sold.'' ’Tis English cloth.
''Nor.'' That ’s a good ''wear'' indeed.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, ii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' An article or articles worn, or intended or fit to be worn; style of dress, adornment, or the like; hence, fashion; vogue.

{{smaller block|''Pom.'' I hope, sir, your good worship will be my bail.
''Lucio.'' No, indeed, will I not, Pompey; it is not the ''wear.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2. 78.}}}}
{{smaller block|Dispatcheth his lacquey to the chamber early to know what her colours are for the day, with purpose to apply his ''wear'' that day accordingly.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The general ''wear'' for all sorts of people is a small Turban.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, II. i. 129.}}}}
'''4.''' Use; usage received in course of being worn or used; the impairment or diminution in bulk, value, efficiency, etc., which results from use, friction, time, or the like.
{{smaller block|This rag of scarlet cloth—for time, and ''wear'', and a sacrilegious moth had reduced it to little other than a rag—on careful examination, assumed the shape of a letter.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 35.}}}}
{{smaller block|A fibre capable of such strain and ''wear'' as that is used only in the making of heroic natures.
{{right|''Lowell'', Garfield.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He might have seen the ''wear''
Of thirty summers.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, III. 336.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Wear and tear''', the loss by wearing; the waste, diminution, decay, or injury which anything sustains by ordinary use: as, the ''wear and tear'' of machinery; the ''wear and tear'' of furniture.}}

'''wear<sup>2</sup>†''' (wēr), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''weren'', ''werien'', ''weorien'' (pret. ''werede''), < AS. ''werian'', guard, defend, protect, = OS. ''werian'', hinder, = OHG. ''werjan'', ''weren'', hinder, obstruct, protect, defend, MHG. ''wern'', ''wergen'', G. ''wehren'', guard, protect, = Icel. ''verja'' = Sw. ''värja'' = Dan. ''værge'', defend, = Goth. ''warjan'', guard, protect; from the root of ''ware''<sup>1</sup>, ''wary''<sup>1</sup>, and so ult. connected with ''ward''<sup>1</sup> and ''guard''.]   '''1.''' To guard; watch, as a gate, etc., so that it is not entered; defend.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fadir, that may do no dere
Goddis comaundement to fullfyll;
For fra all wathes he will vs ''were'',
Whar-so we wende to wirke his wille.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|I set him to ''wear'' the fore-door wi’ the speir while I kept the back-door wi’ the lance.
{{right|''Border Minstrelsy'', i. 208. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}
'''2.''' To ward off; prevent from approaching or entering: as, to ''wear'' the wolf from the sheep. —'''3.''' To conduct or guide with care or caution, as into a fold or place of safety. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Will ye gae to the ewe-buchts, Marion,
And ''wear'' in the sheep wi’ me?</poem>
{{right|''Old Song'', in Ramsay’s Tea-Table Miscellany.}}}}

'''wear'''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.'' See ''weir''.

'''wearable''' (wãr′a̤-bl), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''wear''<sup>1</sup> + ''able.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Capable of being worn; fit for wear, as a garment or a textile fabric.
{{smaller block|Respecting the hereafter of the ''wearable'' fabrics, the furniture, and the walls, we can assert thus much, that they are all in process of decay.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', First Principles, § 93.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A garment; a piece of wearing-apparel.
{{smaller block|The Celt . . . moved off with Mrs. Dutton’s ''wearables'', and deposited the trunk containing them safely in the boat.
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xli.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let a woman ask me to give her an edible or a ''wearable''; . . . I can, at least, understand the demand.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xxiii.}}}}

'''weare''' (wēr), ''n.''   [A spelling of ''wear''<sup>3</sup>, ''weir.'']   In ''her.'', a bearing representing a screen or fence made of wattled twigs, or the like, and upright stakes. It is generally represented in fesse.

'''wearer''' (wãr′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''wear''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who wears, bears, or carries on the body, or as an appendage to the body: as, the ''wearer'' of a cloak, a sword, or a crown.
{{smaller block|<poem>By Jupiter,

'''weariable''' (wēr′i-ạ-bl), ''a.''   [< ''weary''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able.'']   Capable of becoming wearied or fatigued.   ''Quarterly Rev.'' [Rare.]

'''wearied''' (wēr′id), ''p. a.'' Tired; fatigued; exhausted with exertion.
{{smaller block|The Samoeds know these vnknowne deserts, and can tell where the mosse groweth wherewith they refresh their ''wearied'' Deere.

'''weariful''' (wēr′i-fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''weary''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful.'']   An unnecessary extension of ''weary''<sup>1</sup>; perhaps suggested by ''wearisome.''] Full of weariness; causing weariness; wearisome; tiresome; tedious. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I was reading “Polexandre,” the ''wearifullest'' of books, I think; and I heard nothing but the rats and the mice.
{{right|''A. E. Barr'', Friend Olivia, ii.}}}}

'''wearifully''' (wēr′i-fůl-i), ''adv.'' In a weariful manner; wearisomely. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The long night passed slowly and ''wearifully.''
{{right|''W. Black,'' In Far Lochaber, xxiii.}}}}

'''weariless''' (wēr′i-les), ''a.''   [< ''weary'' + ''-less.'']   Incessant; unwearying; unwearied: as, ''weariless'' wings.   ''Hogg.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Beaten and packed
With the flashing flails of ''weariless'' seas.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell,'' Appledore, iii.}}}}

'''wearily''' (wēr′i-li), ''adv.'' In a weary manner; like one fatigued.
{{smaller block|You look ''wearily.'' {{right|''Shak.,'' Tempest, iii. 1. 32.}}}}

'''weariness''' (wēr′i-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''werynes, werinesse, werynesse, werinisse,'' < AS. ''wērignes, wērines,'' weariness, < ''wērig,'' weary: see ''weary'' and ''-ness.'']   '''1.''' The state of being weary or tired; that lassitude or exhaustion of strength which is induced by labor, or lack of sleep or rest; fatigue.
{{smaller block|<poem>After his hunteng and his besynesse,
ffor his travell and his grete ''werynes,''
He felle a slepe. ''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 160.</poem>
We come to a certayne stone vpon ye which our blessyd Lady was wont to rest her ''werynes'' whan she most deuoutly visyted these holy place[s] after ye ascension of or Lord.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde,'' Pylgrymage, p. 33.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Weariness''
Can snore upon the flint, when resty sloth
Finds the down pillow hard.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' Cymbeline, iii. 6. 33.}}}}
{{smaller block|With ''weariness'' and wine oppress’d.
{{right|''Dryden,'' tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xii. 763.}}}}
'''2.''' Mental depression proceeding from monotonous continuance; tedium; ennui; languor. {{smaller block|Till one could yield for ''weariness.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}}
'''3.''' A feeling of dissatisfaction or vexation with something or with its continuance.
{{smaller block|A man would die, though he were neither valiant nor miserable, only upon a ''weariness'' to do the same thing so oft over and over.
{{right|''Bacon'', Death (ed. 1887).}}}}
{{smaller block|The Thirteenth King was Osred, whose Wife Cutburga, out of a loathing ''Weariness'' of Wedlock, sued out a Divorce from her Husband, and built a Nunnery at Winburn in Dorsetshire, where in a Religious Habit she ended her life.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 6.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' ''Lassitude'', etc. See ''fatigue.''

'''wearing''' (wãr′ing), ''n.''   [< ME. ''werung, weriunge''; verbal n. of ''wear''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of one who wears.—'''2.''' That which one wears; clothes; garments.
{{smaller block|Give me my nightly ''wearing'', and adieu.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 3. 16.}}}}
'''3.''' The act of wearing away or passing.
{{smaller block|Now again in a half-month’s ''wearing'' goes Sigrid into the wild.
{{right|''William Morris'', Sigurd, i.}}}}

'''wearing''' (wãr′ing), ''p. a.'' Wasting; consuming; exhausting; tiring: as, ''wearing'' suspense or grief.

'''wearing-apparel''' (wãr′ing-ạ-par″el), ''n.'' Garments worn, or made for wearing; dress in general.

'''wear-iron''' (wãr′ī″ėrn), ''n.'' A friction-guard, consisting of a plate of iron or steel, set on the surface or edge of a softer material to prevent abrasion, as on the edge of the body of a wagon, to prevent the forward wheels from wearing, grinding, or scraping the body in turning. Also ''wear-plate.''

'''wearish†''' (wēr′ish), ''a.''   [Also ''weerish'', ''werish'', ''warish;'' origin uncertain; some confusion with ''weary''<sup>1</sup>, and perhaps with ''waterish'', appears to exist.]   '''1.''' Insipid; tasteless; weak; washy.
{{smaller block|''Werysshe'', as meate is that is nat well tastye — . . . mal sauoré.
{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 328.}}}}
{{smaller block|As ''werishe'' and as vnsauery as beetes.
{{right|''Udall'', tr. of Apophthegms of Erasmus, p. 118. (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''2.''' Withered; wizen; shrunk.
{{smaller block|A wretched ''wearish'' elfe.{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''wearish'' hand,
A bloodless lip.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Love’s Sacrifice, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|A little, ''wearish'' old man, very melancholy by nature.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., To the Reader, p. 2.}}}}

'''wearishness†''', ''n.'' Insipidity.   ''Udall.'' (''Davies.'')

'''wearisome''' (wēr′i-sum), ''a.''   [< ''weary''<sup>1</sup> + ''-some.'']   Causing weariness; tiresome; tedious; irksome; monotonous: as, a ''wearisome'' march; a ''wearisome'' day’s work.
{{smaller block|Alas, the way is ''wearisome'' and long!
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 7. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|God had delivered their souls of the ''wearisome'' burdens of sin and vanity.
{{right|''Penn'', Rise and Progress of Quakers, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Few portions of Spanish literature show anything more stiff and ''wearisome'' than the long declamations and discussions in this dull fiction.
{{right|''Ticknor'', Span. Lit., III. 88.}}}}
